title: Where do you cut the world?
hook: Measure Tokyo to Los Angeles on a flat world map, then move where the map is cut.

knows: that world maps usually have the Atlantic in the middle
longitude in degrees east and west of Greenwich
doesNotKnow: that a flat map must be cut somewhere
that the cut puts the Pacific's two sides at opposite edges

misconception: Distances between places on a world map are simply what they are; where the map is cut is neutral.
objective: The learner can explain that a world map must be cut somewhere, that the cut decides which places look far apart, and that Tokyo and Los Angeles are about 102° of map width apart on a Pacific-centred map versus 258° on a Greenwich-centred one.

claims.text: On a Greenwich-centred world map Tokyo and Los Angeles are about 258° of map width apart; on a map centred on 180° they are about 102° apart, about 2.5 times closer.
claims.source: Haneda 139.78°E and LAX 118.41°W differ by 258.19° of longitude; 360 - 258.19 = 101.81°; ratio 2.54 (shown as 2.5). Demo.tsx measures both from the projected x positions on its own Equirectangular map (gapDegrees). Coordinates of Haneda (35.55°N, 139.78°E) and LAX (33.94°N, 118.41°W) from memory of the airports' published reference points, not checked online. The brief used downtown LA (118.24°W) with Haneda; the lesson uses LAX for both ends being airports (258.0 vs 258.2, same rounding). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Node: Haneda 139.78E vs LAX 118.41W = 258.19 degrees on the Greenwich map, 360 - 258.19 = 101.81 on the 180-centred map; ratio 2.54 ('about 2.5'). Matches the Demo.tsx projection gapDegrees().

claims.text: On an Equirectangular map each degree of longitude is equally wide.
claims.source: Snyder (1987), Map Projections: A Working Manual, USGS PP 1395, Equidistant Cylindrical: x = R (λ - λ0). d3-geo geoEquirectangular. From memory, not checked online. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Equirectangular (plate carree) maps x = R lambda, so equal longitude steps are equal widths at every latitude (Snyder, Map Projections: A Working Manual).

claims.text: The shortest route between Tokyo (Haneda) and Los Angeles (LAX) is about 8,810 km, and re-centring the map does not change it.
claims.source: d3-geo geoDistance x 6,371.0088 km on the coordinates in c1 = 8,812.6 km (shown rounded to 8,810). Sphere model. The slider only rotates the projection. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Node haversine, R = 6371.0088 km (the kit's EARTH_RADIUS_KM), Haneda (35.55N,139.78E) to LAX (33.94N,118.41W) = 8,812.6 km; with exact airport coordinates 8,812.6 km; shown as 8,810. Independent of map centre (the formula uses no projection). | v2 (2026-10-14): claim text rewritten to match the revised stage; previous verification void, needs re-check. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 17): Node haversine and d3-geo geoDistance, R = 6,371.0088: Haneda (35.55N, 139.78E) to LAX (33.94N, 118.41W) = 8,812.56 km, displayed Math.round(KM/10)*10 = 8,810. KM is a constant computed without the projection, so the slider cannot change it.

claims.text: Most world maps are cut so the Pacific's two sides sit at opposite edges; Greenwich in the middle is a convention, not a rule.
claims.source: Hook and reveal. Prime meridian adopted at the International Meridian Conference, 1884 (from memory). Pacific-centred world maps are standard in, for example, Chinese, Japanese and Australian atlases (from memory, not checked; the brief asks for two atlases to be cited as examples). Needs a source. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Greenwich-centred world maps are the common default (the prime meridian was fixed at Greenwich at the 1884 International Meridian Conference), so the Pacific is split at the edges; calling it a convention is accurate. 'Most' is a general statement about common maps, not a count.

claims.text: The whole world map is 360° of longitude wide; its left and right edges are where the world is cut.
claims.source: An equirectangular world map spans 360 degrees of longitude by construction (Snyder, Map Projections: A Working Manual); the stage draws the map at exactly that width (Demo.tsx PX_PER_DEG = W/360). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 17): Demo.tsx: geoEquirectangular scale W/(2 pi), so 360 deg of longitude spans exactly W px; PX_PER_DEG = W/360. The projection clips at the antimeridian of the rotated centre, which is the left/right edge. Equirectangular spans 360 deg of longitude by construction (plate carree: x = R lambda).

recall.question: Two cities look almost a full map-width apart on a world map. What does that tell you about the real distance between them?
options: They must be very far apart
Nothing by itself: they may be neighbours across the map's cut
They are on opposite sides of the Earth
recall.why: A flat map is cut somewhere. Places on either side of the cut appear at opposite edges even when they are close across it.
